title: Halloween Horror Nights Opens at Universal Studios Hollywood With ‘Sinners,’ ‘Stranger Things 5’ and a Blood-Soaked Nikki From ‘Obsession’
description:
Halloween has officially arrived at Universal Studios Hollywood. 

	Halloween Horror Nights opened Thursday at the theme park where screams of excit
body:
Halloween has officially arrived at Universal Studios Hollywood. 

	Halloween Horror Nights opened Thursday at the theme park where screams of excitement turned to screams of fright. Guests rushed into the park to face this year’s collection of haunted houses, which included the Upside Down from Netflix’s “Stranger Things 5” and the vampire-infested Club Juke from “Sinners.”


	Within just 30 minutes of opening, the wait for “Sinners”” had already reached 60 minutes. “Hellraiser,” which made its Halloween Horror Nights debut, had a 50-minute wait, while “Killer Klowns From Outer Space,” “Evil Dead Burn” and “Killceañera: Music by Slash” were each at 30-minutes. “Ozzy Osbourne: Prince of Darkness” reached 35-minutes, and “Stranger Things 5” and “Dead, Deader, Deadest” sat at 25 minutes. 
	

	The scares extended beyond the haunted houses, with characters from this year’s lineup of horror roaming the park. Among them was a crazed, blood-soaked Nikki, from “Obsession.” She emerged from the crowds with the same unnerving affection she carried throughout the film, telling guests she loved them “so, so much” before slipping back into the masses in search of her next victim. Nikki doesn’t have a designated meeting location, instead roaming the park at random. Fans of the film will have to seek her out, or perhaps, Nikki will see vistors out!



	

	



	The most crowded area could be found in the Lower Lot, where Universal paid homage to music legend Ozzy Osbourne. Ozzy’s Bar drew in an approximately hourlong wait by the end of the night, serving themed cocktails such as the Blizzard of Ozz-arita and the Ultimate Sin-ammon, as well as meals including a naan taco named Bark at the Naan. 
	



	

	



	His haunted house, “Ozzy Osbourne: Prince of Darkness,” featured different variants of the musician jumping out to scare visitors, ranging from mad-scientist Ozzy to a demon-esque bat carrying what seemed to be Ozzy’s head. The house also had a room dedicated to “Crazy Train,” where dead bodies sat along a train car while his famous song played in the background. 



	

	



	Also in the Lower Lot was the “Stranger Things 5” haunted house, where guests traveled past Castle Byers and into the Upside Down. Vecna frequently lunged out from hidden corners and windows while a Demogorgon nearby battled Karen Wheeler in her blood-soaked kitchen. 



	

	



	“Sinners,” meanwhile, transports guests into the world of Ryan Coogler’s Oscar-winning film in the Upper Lot. Opening with a performance by Sammie, the haunted house recreates Club Juke, where characters including Mary, Annie and Pearline run rampant. 



	

	



	Also on the Upper Lot was an area dedicated to Fortnite, which drew significant crowds along the walkway as guests stopped to take in the scares and pose in front of the game’s signature Battle Bus. 

	Halloween Horror Nights runs on select nights until Nov. 1.

schema.headline: Halloween Horror Nights Opens at Universal Studios Hollywood With ‘Sinners,’ ‘Stranger Things 5’ and a Blood-Soaked Nikki From ‘Obsession’

title: Meet Topic, the Indie Studio Dominating the Festival Circuit With ‘The Debut,’ ‘Club Kid,’ ‘Wicker’
description: Movies developed and financed outside of the major studios and streamers have a massive hill to climb. It happens that Topic Studios, one such indep
body:
Movies developed and financed outside of the major studios and streamers have a massive hill to climb. It happens that Topic Studios, one such independent shop, has made it all the way up the Rockies — with some of the year’s buzziest films in tow. 

	On the ground at this weekend’s Telluride Film Festival in Colorado, Topic will show Jesse Eisenberg’s anticipated follow-up to “A Real Pain,” the Julianne Moore and Paul Giamatti dramedy “The Debut.” The studio will also let Jordan Firstman’s “Club Kid” out of the gate for the second time after enchanting the Cannes Film Festival in May. In a month, Black Bear will release Topic’s “Wicker” after a successful bow at Sundance in January.Founded in 2017, the company is a division of First Look Media and has been behind some of the most acclaimed projects of the past decade (including Pablo Larrain’s “Spencer,” Michael Angelo Covino’s “The Climb” and the Oscar-winning “Spotlight”). Variety caught up with Topic film and documentary head Ryan Heller to discuss the company’s secret sauce, surviving without M&A and what’s next.

	Topic is on a roll. How did you get here? 


	Ryan Heller: We’ve worked hard over the last few years to identify things that we feel uniquely suited to make happen. In this post-COVID period, which we’re all still living in, we’re figuring out what new the behaviors look like and how movie culture has changed. We’ve leaned into things that resonate with us – on the filmmaker and story level. Things that have a communal aspect. We never take anyone showing up to a movie theater for granted, so we’ve tried to earn their trust.

	How do you think movie culture has changed?
	

	How would you define your palate for story?

	RH: It seems like audiences are showing up for specific movies now, instead of walking into theaters [looking to discover]. We approach the projects we take on by asking how we’re uniquely suited to help. That means projects that are independent as a feature, not a bug. Our responsibility is to figure out how to guide those things to market with a shot at getting the audience they deserve.



	

					Topic Studios film and documentary head Ryan Heller.
	



	RH: Distinctive and filmmaker-driven. Movies that may have to fight to be seen, but in execution can find a sizable audience. We want movies that drive conversation. We’re mostly developing or financing projects on the way to production or financing them through, and we gravitate toward writer-directors. We love that sort of intimacy.

	There seems to be something confrontational about each of these movies, which isn’t necessarily a bad thing. “Splitsville” confronts the terrors of insecurity and marriage. “Club Kid” is about acknowledging self-destruction, in a way, and realizing that better decisions mean more happiness.

	RH: I’m sure there’s truth to that, but it’s not intentional. The hardest thing for us is finding the projects. So, when we see something we fall for it’s the greatest thing. Some of what you’re saying is just inherent to what gets made in the independent system.

	So what makes you “fall for” a project?

	RH: I think we gravitate toward big laughs and big feelings. We love comedies that have the stakes of a drama. That’s why we love “Club Kid” so much. That script knocked us out. We all had expectations of what it was going to be, and every single person at Topic who read that script ended it in tears. And it was all earned. Getting to have a front row seat to how Jordan pulled that off at every stage of production while also acting in almost every scene was really special. It was a career highlight. The same goes for “The Debut” and “Wicker.” They really got us.

	“The Debut” is the hottest ticket in Telluride this year, it seems.

	RH: The expectations are hard to control. I don’t know that we think about them too much. We are truly over the moon excited for people to see this movie. We’ve been working on it since the release of “A Real Pain.” We’ll lean on our great partners at A24 to figure out how we how we get as many people to see the film as possible. We’re counting down the minutes to let this thing loose in front of audiences.

	So you’ve got the hot hand. Are people talking to you about sales and mergers and acquisitions, or are you tuning that out?
	

	RH: We love where we are, and we’ve built such great relationships with so many partners. We focus on being deliberate and going in on things finding ways to be self-reliant. What we’ve built is an internal capability to make a movie from start to finish. There’s a real value to companies like Topic supplying certain kinds of movies to distribution partners. They have different economics than we do. I think we’re part of a healthy ecosystem. We love where we are and want to keep doing it.

	What’s next?

	RH: We have some stuff we haven’t announced yet, but we’re in postproduction on a movie called “Scorn.” It’s from a writer-director named Sarah Bliss, who co-created the series “Search Party.” That’s a house favorite over here. She’s incredible, and it gave a chance to reteam with the incredible Adria Arjona, who we worked with on “Splitsville.” It’s a surprising and very modern take on the psychological erotic thriller. It goes to very unexpected places.

title: Jack Huston Cheers on Paul Schrader as Sexual Abuse Drama ‘Basics of Philosophy’ Premieres in Venice
description: Paul Schrader looked visibly moved as his new film “The Basics of Philosophy,” about a professor confronted with his past sexual abuse, premiered ou
body:
Paul Schrader looked visibly moved as his new film “The Basics of Philosophy,” about a professor confronted with his past sexual abuse, premiered out-of-competition at Venice to a moderate 4.5-minute ovation on Friday night.

	The crowd cheered “Bravi, Bravi!” as star Jack Huston patted him on the back and added to the cheering. Co-stars Sofia Boutella, Bill Pullman and Daniel Zovatto also huddled warmly with the director.


	“The Basics of Philosophy” stars Huston as philosophy professor John Jorissen, who committed a terrible act as a young man. When the victim unexpectedly reappears in his life, he must finally face the consequences of his actions. Alongside Huston, the film also features Boutella, Zovatto, Pullman, Dana Delany, Shiloh Fernandez, Karl Glusman and Elizabeth Petruso.
	

	Variety critic Jessica Kiang noted Huston’s performance in her review of the film, writing, “He is impressive here because of the peculiar intensity of his gaze, the too-smoothly-controlled, cultured timbre of his voice, the general sense of something about him being just that bit off.”

	“The Basics of Philosophy” marks Schrader’s latest “man in a room” story, focusing on troubled men who struggle with guilt and seek redemption. In a press conference earlier on Friday, Schrader said that his upbringing as a Calvinist has influenced his cinematic obsession with these topics.

	“My childhood was one of predestination, guilt, total depravity and all that,” Schrader said. “I don’t know how I do not write about guilt and redemption.”

	The 80-year-old writer and director, best known for penning “Taxi Driver” and for helming films including “American Gigolo” and “First Reformed,” is no stranger to Venice Film Festival. “First Reformed,” “The Card Counter” and “Master Gardener” all premiered at the fest, and in 2022, Schrader received a Golden Lion for Lifetime Achievement. 
	

	Martin Scorsese boarded “The Basics of Philosophy” as an executive producer ahead of the film’s Venice launch. The film is produced by Braxton Pope and David Wulf.

title: ‘Tender Loving Care’ Review: Mike Leigh’s Tale of Social Workers, Lonely Hearts and Dementia Should Have Been a Fuller Portrait
description: Every so often, the British writer-director Mike Leigh makes a movie in which the stars — and the tartly casual dramatic scenes — line up, coalescin
body:
Every so often, the British writer-director Mike Leigh makes a movie in which the stars — and the tartly casual dramatic scenes — line up, coalescing into a full-on vision of prickly humanity. It happened in “Secrets & Lies” (1996), admittedly a kind of “Guess Who’s Coming to Dinner” for the art-house crowd, though in its neorealist-sitcom way it was a movie that fired on all cylinders. It happened in “Topsy-Turvy” (1999), Leigh’s sublime Gilbert and Sullivan biopic — easily his greatest film, which is quite the irony given that it’s the furthest he ever strayed from his working-class fixations. It happened, too, in “Another Year” (2010), his scaldingly funny riff on the melancholy of middle age.
	

	“Tender Loving Care,” I’m compelled to report, is not one of those Leigh movies where it all comes together for him, fusing into a drama that’s greater than the sum of its parts. This one has a handful of vivid characters who are lively and touching company. The actors, as is always the case in a Mike Leigh film, inhabit their roles with uncanny everyday verve. You might say, “What’s not to like?” But Watching “Tender Loving Care,” I had the sense of wanting Leigh to go deeper into his characters — into the dreams holding their lives together, and the trauma underlying their daily grind. Leigh doesn’t make any wrong moves here; just about every scene in the movie plays. Yet “Tender Loving Care” builds (or maybe I should say recedes) to something more schematic than it is powerful.


	The title sounds inviting, but what does it mean? It refers to about five different things at once, and that fuzziness is actually a bit of problem, in terms of cueing the audience to what the film is about. Amy (Kate O’Flynn), the spiky-on-the-surface but really quite winsome central character, and her best friend, the more merciless but superficial Rosie (Alice Bailey Johnson), are social workers, so they’ve dedicated their lives to helping people — but the tender loving care they offer is starting to fall on deaf ears. Amy has the look of a beaming nun: smiling, devotional, hair pulled back in a way that’s a touch prim. We see her attempt to engage one emotionally lost teen foster child after another, but they’re not engaging with her. Amy still cares, but does the system care? The background of the film is the budget slashes that are happening in this sector all over the Western world, as the government withdraws its own form of care.
	

	“Tender loving care” also refers to how Amy and Rosie take care of each other. Amy has moved back into Rosie’s comfy apartment after five years, during which Amy was living with a man; but now he’s abandoned her and gone back to his wife in Glasgow. The two women start to hang out again like college pals, gossiping and hip-hip dancing and — always – splitting a bottle of white wine. They’ve been friends for decades and care deeply about each other. But do they care, in the right way, about themselves?

	Amy’s aging parents are presented as the Platonic ideal of caring. They’re utterly conventional middle-class fuddy-duddies who have always treated Amy, their only child, with kid gloves (and they still do, even though she’s 37). Marion Bailey, who plays the mum, is Leigh’s real-life partner, and she creates an infectious portrait of nattering devotion. But it’s Paul Jesson, as her husband (the character must be approaching 80 but looks even older), who makes the film’s most starkly moving impression. He’s the soul of decency, wrapped in a hard crust. He’s the kind of relative you love to see on holidays, because he doesn’t have much to say. But in his doddering way, he’s all there. (He tells jokes.) Until he isn’t. The onset of his dementia arrives slowly but surely (as these things tend to do), and Leigh is too sly a filmmaker to milk it. “Tender Loving Care” says to its audience: Yes, this happens. And when it does, the person you know is gone, just like that. (Jesson’s character starts talking about swans.) That, more than ever, is when we need care.

	It’s an intermittently compelling, mildly affecting, in the end slightly scattershot movie. The reason I’m sounding a bit churlish about it is that it engages us without touching any hidden glimmer of mystery in its characters, any surprise perception of pain or desire. Amy and Rosie are intensely appealing women, yet their lives with men have been a washout. We think: Why? Is it because men are shits? That’s the conclusion the two seem to have come to, especially after the fireman Rosie has her current hopes pinned on asks her out to a fancy dinner date, only to stand her up. But this double lonely-hearts scenario is too sodden and limiting. Even if these women aren’t happy (or lucky in love), the film needed to give us a more developed feeling for what they want.
	

	The most starkly powerful scene in the film is about motherhood. One of Amy’s charges is a mess of a young mother who has had all three of her children taken away from her by the state. She’s scared to talk to Amy because she thinks what she says will just be used against her. Is she right? What’s Leigh’s attitude here? It should have been clearer, but what comes across with utter force is the character’s life-and-death passion.

	Amy needed a moment like that. Kate O’Flynn, from the TV series “Widow’s Bay,” is a commanding actor, but she doesn’t invest Amy with the power of a destiny laid bare. And that’s because Leigh isn’t totally invested in her destiny; he wants to tie it all into a larger “sociological” view. The film opens with Rosie interviewing an old demented homeless man in a hospital, and then, the morning after, he has vanished, fallen through the cracks of the system. He comes back at the end — and we can’t help but notice that he looks like the man Jesson’s character might have been, if he’d had no one to take care of him. I guess that makes a statement. But it’s an abstract statement. It tweaks our pieties rather than roiling our souls.

schema.headline: ‘Tender Loving Care’ Review: Mike Leigh’s Tale of Social Workers, Lonely Hearts and Dementia Should Have Been a Fuller Portrait

title: Jennifer Lawrence Says ‘I Can’t Do a Lot’ of Botox Because ‘I Need to Have Movement in My Face’ as an Actor, So ‘I Get Baby Botox’
description: Jennifer Lawrence opened up to Vogue about her relationship to cosmetic procedures and said she resists going overboard when it comes to botox becau
body:
Jennifer Lawrence opened up to Vogue about her relationship to cosmetic procedures and said she resists going overboard when it comes to botox because she is a working actor and facial movement is of the upmost important. The Oscar winner’s comment was published just a few weeks after Olivia Wilde put the industry on blast, telling Vogue that “it’s not easy” to find actresses to cast in movies because many of them can no longer move their faces.
	

	“I can’t really get very much done,” Lawrence told Vogue. “I need to have movement in my face — I get baby Botox, but I can’t do a lot. If my skin is going to be a little saggier than I would like, at least it looks dewy and pretty.” 


	Regarding the procedures she is hesitant to try, Lawrence said: “Oh, I’m really nervous about these fat transfers. I support other people doing them because I want to continue to watch and see what happens, but I don’t know about that. I mean, I would love to have a buccal fat removal. I can’t because everybody would know, but just know that I want that.”

	“I do like the radiofrequency because I have huge cheeks and so I feel like exercising them as much as possible,” she added.

	Olivia Wilde appeared on an episode of “The Run-Through with Vogue” during her summer press tour for “The Invite” when she noted: “As a director, I now am constantly searching for actresses who can still move their faces, and it’s not easy… I am a product of the same machine. I am under the same pressures. I get it.” 

	“There’s something so medieval about a lot of these things,” she added at the time. “I’ve had the thing of people being like, ‘She looks old and dead and awful.’ And you’re like, ‘Fuck! How do you win? It’s impossible.'”
	

	Lawrence was a fixture on last year’s awards circuit as the star of “Die My Love,” which premiered at Cannes and earned her a Golden Globe nomination for best actress in a motion picture drama. She’s expected to appear as her “Hunger Games” character Katniss Everdeen in a small role in this November’s prequel movie “Sunrise on the Reaping.” Lawrence’s next big headlining role is opposite Leonardo DiCaprio’s in Martin Scorsese’s “What Happens at Night.” The film is expected to arrive next year.

schema.headline: Jennifer Lawrence Says ‘I Can’t Do a Lot’ of Botox Because ‘I Need to Have Movement in My Face’ as an Actor, So ‘I Get Baby Botox’

title: Jay-Z Brings Out Lauryn Hill and Wyclef at ‘Jay-Z30’ London Concert
description: Jay-Z’s “Jay-Z30” tour has been filled with guest appearances and his opening night at London’s Tottenham Hotspur Stadium was no exception: He broug
body:
Jay-Z’s “Jay-Z30” tour has been filled with guest appearances and his opening night at London’s Tottenham Hotspur Stadium was no exception: He brought out Lauryn Hill and Wyclef for a mini-Fugees reunion on their 1995 hit “Ready or Not,” and, in a nod to local talent, South London rapper Giggs after shouting him out in song.

	He also shined a spotlight on his wife Beyonce in one of the stadium’s boxes, as it was her birthday (which she herself observed by releasing a 20 th anniversary edition of her 2006 album “Bday” on Friday). However, she did not join him onstage.
	


	Jay’s three concerts at Yankee Stadium in July featured a staggering number of guests — 19 in all — including Beyonce, their daughter Blue Ivy, Rihanna, Eminem, Nas, Alicia Keys, Pharrell, Usher, Swizz Beatz, Teyana Taylor and more.



	Jay is slated to perform on Saturday night as well, and will follow with a concert at Paris’ Stade de France on Sept. 10 and a pair of shows at Los Angeles’ SoFi Stadium on October 23 and 24.

	The extra shows come amid an active year for Jay-Z, who made a grand return to the stage earlier this year with a headlining performance at the Roots Picnic in Philadelphia. During that performance, he toured his catalog and brought out a slew of native guests including Beanie Sigel, Freeway, Memphis Bleek, Jazmine Sullivan, Bilal and Young Gunz.

	Amid his busy year, Jay-Z is set to sit down with Rick Rubin for the eight-part documentary series “Jay-Z in 8,” debuting on HBO this fall. Rubin is directing the series and will interview the rapper about his music, lyrics, life experiences and creative process.

schema.headline: Jay-Z Brings Out Lauryn Hill and Wyclef at ‘Jay-Z30’ London Concert

title: Jordan Firstman’s ‘Club Kid’ Hits Telluride, and Colleen Camp Could Be Its Secret Oscar Weapon
description:
Jordan Firstman is hoping to join an exclusive club: the Oscars. And he might have someone on his team that can help him do it.

	“Club Kid,” Firstm
body:
Jordan Firstman is hoping to join an exclusive club: the Oscars. And he might have someone on his team that can help him do it.

	“Club Kid,” Firstman’s directorial debut, arrived in Cannes’ Un Certain Regard section and drew a six-minute standing ovation before A24 acquired it for a reported $17 million. Suddenly, one of the internet’s more recognizable comic personalities — currently a regular on Rachel Sennott’s comedy series “I Love L.A.” — had a movie, a major distributor and a fall festival trajectory far more serious than anyone might have expected. It bowed at the Telluride Film Festival on Friday night with much anticipation for those who weren’t on the Croisette, and the film is ready to make its big splash on the circuit.
	

	That’s the first awards story. The second may belong to one of his co-stars, Colleen Camp.


	Firstman writes, directs and stars as Peter, a washed-up New York party promoter whose life on the dance floor screeches to a halt when the 10-year-old son (played by the exquisite British newcomer Reggie Absolom) he never knew existed turns up on his doorstep. The premise invites the easy shorthand — a gay “Big Daddy” — but Firstman uses it as a way into something more complete. It’s a study of responsibility, loneliness and the possibility that adulthood might begin long after you’ve stopped expecting it. The film works on three fronts with a touching script, naturalistic direction and a genuinely endearing lead turn.

	A24’s fall strategy only heightens the opportunity. The company is running “Club Kid” through Telluride before heading to Toronto and New York ahead of a November release, which is the classic runway for a movie built to play as a crowd-pleaser rather than a critics’ curiosity.
	

	This is where Camp comes in — the veteran embedded in the ensemble whom many still aren’t clocking as the film’s secret weapon.

	At 73, Camp is a character actress-turned-social connector whose close friends include half the A-listers in town. By many estimates, she’s a significant reason Andrea Riseborough landed that shocking best actress nomination for “To Leslie.” Da’Vine Joy Randolph even thanked her by name from the Oscar stage while winning for “The Holdovers.” In recent years, Camp has become an influential operator on the circuit, with high-powered parties, star-studded dinners and taste-making events that have redirected more Oscar campaigns than anyone will admit on the record. Think Countess Luann from “The Real Housewives of New York,” but with real sway over the people at her table. She’s part of the reason a healthy share of today’s Oscar nominees and winners got there at all, which is exactly why it would be foolish to discount her now.



	

									Adam Newport-Berra
	



	But long before she was hosting the parties, Camp was working the sets. A Hollywood lifer whose credits run from “Apocalypse Now” to “Clue,” she has spent five decades inhabiting roles that make movies richer without turning into awards contenders. In fact, she has only two award nominations on her IMDb page — from the Razzie Awards — “The Seduction” (1982) and “Sliver” (1993). Wouldn’t it be heartwarming to see that rectified in a meaningful way?

	In addition, she turns up twice in A24’s awards corridor, also appearing in Chris Rock’s “Misty Green,” which is just more visibility.

	That could make “Club Kid” a particularly appealing vehicle, and one that awards pundits shouldn’t underestimate. The best comeback narratives aren’t manufactured. They tend to emerge when an actor with a real body of work lands a part that reminds everyone why they loved watching them in the first place. Camp’s turn here as a kooky neighbor who stumbles into an unexpected romance is exactly the kind of role that gets a room talking (and laughing).

	The challenge here is scale, because she doesn’t have a ton of screen time. Not to mention, a scene stealer isn’t automatically an Oscar performance, especially in a supporting actress field expected to be overly crowded. A24 would have to convert the affection for Camp, and the film, into a sustained argument about the work, not merely leaning on nostalgia.
	

	But nostalgia isn’t nothing. Voters love a rediscovery story, especially when it’s attached to a movie they actually enjoyed. “Club Kid” may offer the rare double with two generations of Hollywood recognition at once; Firstman is the new face arriving from the internet, and Camp, the veteran whose face the establishment already knows.

schema.headline: Jordan Firstman’s ‘Club Kid’ Hits Telluride, and Colleen Camp Could Be Its Secret Oscar Weapon

title: ‘Silo’ Season 3 Finale: Rebecca Ferguson, Creator Graham Yost on That Twist and Why Juliette Is ‘S–t Scared!’ Going Into the Final Season
description:
SPOILER ALERT: This post contains spoilers from “Troy,” the Season 3 finale of “Silo,” now streaming on Apple TV.

	In the Season 3 finale of Apple
body:
SPOILER ALERT: This post contains spoilers from “Troy,” the Season 3 finale of “Silo,” now streaming on Apple TV.

	In the Season 3 finale of Apple TV’s “Silo,” an amnesia-stricken Juliette (Rebecca Ferguson) finally regains her memories just in time to declare war. But first, she confronts the disembodied voice behind The Algorithm, the malevolent force controlling the silos. With milliseconds to spare, her team of Silo 18 misfits and former leaders — herself included in both distinctions — managed to cap the safeguard, a pipe that would have flooded their silo with toxic gas and killed its nearly 10,000 residents for their insolence.



	

									Courtesy of Apple TV
	



	But viewers now know who is on the other end of that threat: Daniel Keene (Ashley Zukerman), the once-idealistic congressman who sought refuge in the newly opened silos when the bombs went off in the season’s penultimate episode last week. Now decades (centuries?) later, he is known as Troy, and he’s periodically awoken from a cryogenic slumber to make some cold-hearted decisions about what to do when silos go rogue and ask too many questions. He doesn’t recognize his own sister Charlotte (Jessica Brown Findlay), he commits genocide with a second thought and he doesn’t like being bested by Juliette.

	But with the pipe capped, Daniel and Silo 18 are at a stand off. When Juliette, Shirley (Remmie Milner), Knox (Shane McRae), Camille (Alexandria Riley) and Deputy Murphy (Billy Postlethwaite) venture down to the sealed-off tunnel that connects all the silos, Daniel as the omni-present voice all but congratulates them on outsmarting The Algorithm. Knowing they are trapped inside, Daniel offers a truce to let them live in peace — until their rapidly dwindling resources run out, at least. Knowing that he almost certainly doesn’t mean it, Juliette accepts, and retreats her team to strategize. But one thing is clear: This is war.

	Ferguson tells Variety that Juliette keeps her cool in that moment, “But I think she’s shit scared!” she says. “Sometimes it’s hard to come up with all the solutions because no one else is.”


	How Juliette and company plan to fend off The Algorithm when they barely know anything about the purposes of the silos, the history of other failed rebellions or who they are even fighting will be the crux of the fourth and final season, which series creator Graham Yost confirms has already been shot and will pick up mere hours after the Season 3 finale. On Friday, Apple TV released a teaser of the show’s fourth and final season, and announced it will premiere on July 9, 2027.



	Ahead of that final season, Ferguson and Yost break down the finale, the uncomfortable journey of Juliette the hero, whether viewers might see some of these other failed silo rebellions — and who might see the night sky by the end.

	
		Rebecca, you spent two seasons with Juliette being this ascendant but reluctant leader. This season, she doesn’t have any memory of that. Reflecting on Season 3 as a whole, how was it clawing your way back to her sense of self?	

	Rebecca Ferguson: I think memory loss is an interesting one, because you’re not really aware of your being. So there is such a powerful underline of her character, this sort of fierce rebel constantly wanting to find out the truth, constantly aware of her surroundings, aware of everything. I sometimes feel she’s a bit like Jason Bourne — she clocks everything. It was fun playing it, because it’s challenging to do. But the fun moments were the moments where something happened, and we had to figure out, how important is this on a scale of one to 10? How much does it affect her, what is the memory storyline. We even had Shelley [Birse], one of the writers, break down just the memory bit, so it all made sense, because it’s difficult to hold everything.
	



	

									Courtesy of Apple TV
	


	
		But instinctively now, she gravitates toward being a leader. Even without her memories, she slowly assumes that position again by this finale.	

	Ferguson: Graham said it so well: She’s a leader with no power. She hasn’t chosen this, she never chooses to be the sheriff, she kind of accepts it because she’s looking for something. The ripple effects make her a leader, but I don’t think she would position herself as a leader even now. She is a truth finder.

	Graham Yost: That’s all she cares about — finding out the truth and looking for, perhaps, freedom. One of the most fun things we came up with in the room were the fan girls [to show how people see Juliette as a leader]. We loved it because we knew it would make Rebecca uncomfortable.
	

	Ferguson: Oh, I hated it!

	Yost: It was just so cool to have the young women all dressed up like Juliette the leader. But another thing that just came to me is that in the writers’ room, we always talk about how Juliette has to learn something in every season. In Season 2, she has to learn how to work with someone because she has to rely on Solo [Steve Zahn], and then finds out that’s not even his name. She needs something, and she also needs to help him, and the fact that she steps up for him still makes me very emotional. But in Season 3, she has to find out who she is, and she has to rely on other people. That’s not easy for someone who’s a “I’m gonna pick up the wrench and fix it myself” kind of person. She has to rely on her friends to solve the big problem at the end of the season.

	Ferguson: Without actually knowing who her friends are.

	Yost: Exactly! But the successful capping of the safeguard at the end of the season, that was all done by other people and she had to rely on that.
	
		How was it for you, Rebecca, to allow Juliette to let others step up for her?	

	Ferguson: I had difficulties. I sometimes merged into her on set. I would fight it. I’d be like, “But why wouldn’t she do that, Graham? Why would she let people do it? I wouldn’t just sit here waiting.” And then he’s like, “Well, what can you actually do here?” I don’t know but you write it because I can’t just sit around! 
	
	
		Even Juliette’s role this season is something she doesn’t really choose, but rather just goes along with when she is made mayor. She doesn’t quite know how to wear it, which is probably why she has completely shed it by the end of the season.	

	Ferguson: I had to put that bloody frock on, and I had little high-heeled shoes. I just remember being like, “This isn’t Juliette.” I started walking like me in high-heeled shoes, and I couldn’t do it. So, in some scenes, I would put my old boots on, so I could have the walk, because nothing in her body would change even if she lost her memories. But that juxtaposition is so great, having jewels in the frock.



	

									Courtesy of Apple TV
	


	
		War is declared by the end of the finale, but one soldier is gone. Bernard (Tim Robbins) was sent out to clean and dies moments later, for real this time. For longtime viewers, Tim’s exit is surreal. But what does the former embodiment of oppression’s death mean for those who came to like him?	

	Yost: He ends up being this inspiration to a number of people who just never believed he would be an inspiration. For us as writers, performers, it was important to see a character that we had really feared and hated, but now realize he was lied to as much as anyone. Initially he gave up, though. He was going to go out to clean, and when the pain got too much, he was going to kill himself, right? But as he says to Juliette, “You happened.” So now he’s had a reason to keep going, and then he gives his life to try and win. To let the good guys win.
	
		What is the state of Silo 18 at the end of Season 3? You have Juliette and her faction, who, as she says at the end, need to take the battle to Silo 1. Is the rest of Silo 18 ready for a war? 	

	Ferguson: Were we ever prepared? 
	
		That’s an incredibly vague tease for the future. But you’ve shot Season 4, correct?	

	Both: Yep!
	
		More than previous seasons, this season felt like half the story. The first of a two-chapter ending, if you will. How much time will pass between Season 3 and Season 4?	

	Yost: Season 4 picks up, literally, three hours after the finale.



	

									Courtesy of Apple TV
	


	
		Moving forward, after their really beautiful walkie-talkie conversation, do you think Juliette is ready or even interested in acknowledging any feelings she has for Lukas (Avi Nash)?	

	I think there are so few people in her life that crack her, who can actually decode her. Walker [Harriet Walter] being No. 1. George was one, and Shirley kind of can, but is more a mate. But Lucas has a possibility of tapping into the vulnerability and seeing something. He’s the one who will push her further. He holds space for her, which is uncomfortable, but it’s also a safety net. It’s familiar, so someone she would lean to, and someone who’s very intelligent, who can help her solve big issues and problems throughout. 
	
		The moment when he finally goes outside and gets to look at the stars was a beautiful acknowledgment of their conversation before. It feels like Juliette would have done something similar had she been outside at night. If nothing else, they feel like kindred spirits in curiosity.	

	Ferguson: Hmm, can you imagine what a moment that would be? [Looks to Yost]
	

	Yost: Wouldn’t that be great if Juliette went out to see the stars at night? Hmm…

	Ferguson: Just pay attention. There’s a Season 4 coming.
	
		So we can file that tease away for when Season 4 comes out. Throughout this season, Camille and her conversations with The Algorithm make mention of other rebellions. Graham, could we see those bits of history come into play in Season 4?	

	Yost: It would be interesting, wouldn’t it, Rebecca? [They both laugh.] Yeah, there’s stuff to come. There was a joke [in the writers’ room], about what was happening in the other silos, and the musical silos are 5678. Get it? We were really proud of that one! And there was a question of where all the plumbing goes. Of course, it is Silo 13. But to answer your question, yes, there is stuff coming about the other silos.

	Ferguson: It will all make sense by the end of Season 4. 

	Yost: We hope. Unless we totally screwed the pooch.
	
		Rebecca, you’ve already shot Season 4, so this might be a tough one. But coming out of Season 3 and looking to the end of this series, what did you want for Juliette as a character? What can fans hold onto that awaits her?	

	Ferguson: There’s something very lonely for Juliette in the beginning of Season 3 with the memory loss and not knowing people, to then gradually get to know them and understand that there are actually people out there who are trying to fight to bring her back. But there are also the powers that be who are gaining profit from her loss. It is a constant struggle for her, but here at the end, we get together. The group is together, she’s not lonely. There’s something about being united for her. But I think she’s shit scared. Sometimes it’s hard to come up with all the solutions because no one else is.
	

	Yost: It was a huge Juliette moment for us that she’s talked to The Algorithm — they’ve gone down to the tunnel at the bottom of the silo and supposedly made a truce. But she says, they’re not going to stand by it, and we’re not. Basically, they now have the responsibility to not just to save themselves, but to save any other silos. If they can do this to any silo, we have that responsibility to stop them. [Looks at Ferguson] You’re the hero now.

	This interview has been edited and condensed.

schema.headline: ‘Silo’ Season 3 Finale: Rebecca Ferguson, Creator Graham Yost on That Twist and Why Juliette Is ‘S–t Scared!’ Going Into the Final Season

title: ‘Wheel of Fortune’ Announcer Jim Thornton Fired by Sony
description: “Wheel of Fortune” announcer Jim Thornton has been fired from the game show, producer Sony Pictures TV confirmed. “Following a thorough investigatio
body:
“Wheel of Fortune” announcer Jim Thornton has been fired from the game show, producer Sony Pictures TV confirmed. “Following a thorough investigation, Jim Thornton’s employment with ‘Wheel of Fortune’ has been terminated, effective immediately,” the studio said in a statement.

	According to insiders, Thornton won’t be heard on the show when it returns for a new season on September 14, as an interim announcer has revoiced all of Thornton’s parts on the shows. No permanent replacement has been announced.
	

	Thornton’s firing came just hours after TMZ posted photos of what were allegedly him on an American Airlines plane with his laptop opened on “disturbing chat room” that appeared to be “images and texts that made it appear it was a chat room for pedophiles.” The up-close photos of the laptop’s screen showed lewd conversations about minors.


	The alleged incident took place in May, when according to TMZ, a passenger informed a flight attendant about the chat screen on Thornton’s laptop. Authorities were waiting to question Thornton when his flight landed at LAX, and after they spoke to the Thornton he was given permission to leave.

	Neither Thornton nor his lawyer have publicly addressed the allegations; an attorney who said they represented the announcer, Allison Hart, told TMZ that Thornton had “become active in suicide-prevention advocacy since losing a close family member to suicide two years ago and he has spent time visiting chat rooms offering support to individuals suffering from suicidal ideation.”

	On Tuesday, Sony Pictures TV said that “we have recently been made aware of allegations concerning Jim Thornton. He has been suspended from ‘Wheel of Fortune’ and we are recasting while we conduct a thorough investigation.” 
	

	The announcer joined “Wheel” in 2010 after the death of the show’s previous announcer, Charlie O’Donnell, and has also worked as a substitute announcer on “The Price Is Right.” He’s also been the voice of “Celebrity Wheel of Fortune” on ABC.

	Thornton’s other credits include “Celebrity Deathmatch,” where he voiced Johnny Gomez, and as an announcer on “The Cleveland Show” and “Tim & Eric Awesome Show, Great Job!” He’s also been heard on several video games and appeared as a commercial narrator in the 2001 animated film “Monsters, Inc.” He also voiced the 2011 Oscar-nominated short animated film “Let’s Pollute.”

	Thornton has been a local media presence in Los Angeles for decades, having previously worked as an afternoon anchor on KNX 1070 Newsradio, which he first joined in 1985 as a traffic reporter with Metro Traffic. He also provided traffic reports on KCBS-TV.

	His other broadcast credits include Westwood One Radio Networks, and he was the voice of L.A.’s KCOP-TV for four years. He has received an Edward R. Murrow award, Golden Mike awards and an Emmy.

body:
Sep 4, 2026 2:20pm PT	
	

	
		17 Best Movies New to Streaming in September: ‘Toy Story 5,’ ‘Backrooms,’ ’Scary Movie 6,’ ’The Mandalorian and Grogu’
	
	
			


			
			
	

									Everett Collection 
	

		
	
				

	Labor Day Weekend brings to a close the summer movie season, which became one of the biggest on record thanks to the mega-blockbusters “The Odyssey” and “Spider-Man: Brand New Day.” But the season is just getting started on streaming platforms as some of the summer’s buzziest titles make their streaming debuts to kick off the fall movie corridor. 

	“Toy Story 5” is the third highest-grossing movie of the year with $1.13 billion and should prove to be a streaming mega-hit when it arrives on Disney+ near the end of the month. Expect the whole “Toy Story” animated franchise to get a streaming lift as a result. A24’s horror hit “Backrooms,” which became the studio’s highest-grossing title in history this summer, should also prove a streaming hit when it lands on HBO Max. Meanwhile, the “Star Wars” misfire “The Mandalorian and Grogu” hopes to rebound on Disney+ after stumbling in theaters. The movie is now available to stream, as is Paramount’s “Scary Movie 6.”

	Check out a full rundown below of the biggest new titles to streaming in September.


			
			
	Toy Story 5 (Sept. 23 on Disney+)
			
										
					Image Credit: ©Walt Disney Co./Courtesy Everett Collection				
					
				
	Disney and Pixar’s animated blockbuster “Toy Story 5” arrives on Disney+ this month after earning $1.13 billion and counting at the summer box office, which makes it the third highest-grossing movie of 2026 so far (trailing “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” and “The Odyssey”). The sequel was also named one of Variety’s best movies of the year so far: “It escalates in delight (the climactic wedding ceremony must be seen to be believed), but it also has moments that hit you like a gut punch. The message is: Slow down, be real and play. The fun you take is equal to the fun you make.”
		
			
			
	Backrooms (Sept. 25 on HBO Max)
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy Everett Collection				
					
				
	Kane Parsons’ horror smash “Backrooms” arrives on HBO Max this month after becoming A24’s highest-grossing movie of all time with $394 million at the worldwide box office. “As an atmospheric freakout, ‘Backrooms’ is extraordinarily effective,” Variety‘s chief film critic Owen Gleiberman wrote in his positive review, noting that Chiwetel Ejiofor was “the perfect presence to have at the center.” He also compared Parsons’ fixation for mood and “cosmic sound design” to the late David Lynch.
		
			
			
	The Mandalorian and Grogu (Disney+)
			
										
					Image Credit: ©Walt Disney Co./Courtesy Everett Collection				
					
				
	“The Mandalorian and Grogu” suffered at the summer box office with an $81 million domestic debut, an underwhelming start for a “Star Wars” movie. The film went on to earn $345 million worldwide, far below the billion-dollar grosses of the previous “Star Wars” film releases “The Rise of Skywalker” and “The Last Jedi.” But can “The Mandalorian and Grogu” rebound on streaming? Directed by Jon Favreau, the movie follows bounty hunter Din Djarin (Pedro Pascal) and his apprentice, Grogu, as they’re recruited by officer Colonel Ward (Sigourney Weaver) to aid the New Republic. The unlikely duo must rescue the heir to Jabba the Hutt, Rotta the Hutt (voiced by “The Bear’s” Jeremy Allen White), in order to track down an Imperial leader.
		
			
			
	Scary Movie (Paramount+) 
			
										
					Image Credit: ©Paramount/Courtesy Everett Collection				
					
				
	“Scary Movie,” also known as “Scary Movie 6,” is now streaming on Paramount+ after delighting the box office with a strong $231 million worldwide. An extended cut of the movie is also now streaming on the same platform. Returning cast members include Marlon Wayans (Shorty Meeks), Shawn Wayans (Ray), Anna Faris (Cindy Campbell) and Regina Hall (Brenda Meeks). Faris and Hall reprised their roles after neither appeared in “Scary Movie 5.”
		
			
			
	Supergirl (Sept. 10 on HBO Max)
			
										
					Image Credit: ©Warner Bros/Courtesy Everett Collection				
					
				
	“Supergirl” soars to streaming on HBO Max on Sept. 10. There will also be an American Sign Language (ASL) version of “Supergirl” available to stream performed by Catalene Sacchetti (“Songs in Sign Language”) and directed by Jonaz McMillan (“The Pitt with ASL” Season One). Directed by Craig Gillespie and written by Ana Nogueira, the adaptation is based on the DC comic series “Supergirl: Woman of Tomorrow” by Tom King. In the comic, Supergirl and a young alien girl named Ruthye travel across the galaxy to hunt down Krem of the Yellow Hill after he murders Ruthye’s father.
		
			
			
	Why Did I Get Married Again? (Sept. 9 on Netflix)
			
										
					Image Credit: ©Netflix/Courtesy Everett Collection				
					
				
	Per Netflix: “In Tyler Perry’s ‘Why Did I Get Married Again?’, the couples reunite in celebration as Marcus and Angela’s daughter prepares to tie the knot. After being apart for quite some time, they learn quickly that as much as things change, they stay the same. Realizing their children have grown up to be so much like them, they must reflect on the examples they’ve set and ask themselves that age-old question, why did they get married… again?” The cast includes Tyler Perry, Taraji P. Henson, Jill Scott, Richard T. Jones, Tasha Smith, Michael Jai White, Sharon Leal and more.
		
			
			
	Unabomber (Sept. 25 on Netflix)
			
										
					Image Credit: ©Netflix/Courtesy Everett Collection				
					
				
	“Room” breakout Jacob Tremblay is all grown up in Netflix’s “Unabomber,” where he stars in the title role. The movie tracks Ted Kaczynski’s transformation from 16-year-old Harvard prodigy into the infamous Unabomber. Per Netflix: “Subjected to controversial psychological experiments by Professor Henry Murray (Russell Crowe), Kaczynski’s troubled past resurfaces decades later when his manhunt, led by FBI agent Joanne Miller (Shailene Woodley), brings to light the chilling consequences of ambition and isolation.”
		
			
			
	Call My Agent! The Movie (Sept. 10 on Netflix)
			
										
					Image Credit: ©Netflix/Courtesy Everett Collection				
					
				
	Camille Cottin and the rest of the “Call My Agent!” gang return for the feature film follow-up. Per Netflix: “Five years after the agency closed its doors, Andréa is finally ready to direct her first feature film. When her lead actor quits and she falls out with her producer, she joins forces with Noémie—now a successful reality TV producer—believing she can easily manipulate her. But as she faces a complete recasting, on-set disasters, and a legal battle threatening the custody of her daughter, everything begins to unravel.”
		
			
			
	The Love Hypothesis (Sept. 23 on Prime Video)
			
										
					Image Credit: ©Amazon/Courtesy Everett Collection				
					
				
	 Lili Reinhart and Tom Bateman hope to deliver a romance knockout for Amazon Prime Video with the launch of “The Love Hypothesis,” based on the best-selling novel by Ali Hazelwood. Per the synopsis: “Olive (Reinhart), a brilliant Ph.D. candidate focused on her future in academia, realizes her best friend Ahn (Rachel Marsh) has fallen for her crush Jeremy (Nicholas Duvernay), so Olive impulsively kisses intimidating professor Adam Carlsen (Tom Bateman) to prove she’s moved on. What begins as a desperate act of friendship spirals into a fake relationship with rules, boundaries, and a mutually beneficial agreement.”
		
			
			
	Stop That Train (Sept. 20 on Netflix)
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy Everett Collection				
					
				
	Directed by Adam Shankman, “Stop That Train!” stars RuPaul as President Gagwell and “Drag Race” alumni Ginger Minj and Jujubee as best friends who work on the glitzy Glamazonian Express train. When a catastrophic “Stormaganza” threatens to derail the high-speed locomotive and crash it into Los Angeles, the duo in coach must join forces with the snobby first class attendants (Raven-Symone, Brooke Lynn Hytes, Marcia Marcia Marcia) to save the day. Matt Rogers, Sarah Michelle Gellar, Rachel Bloom, Lisa Rinna and Nicole Richie also star in the film.
		
			
			
	The Runner (Sept. 2 on Prime Video)
			
										
					Image Credit: ©Amazon/Courtesy Everett Collection				
					
				
	Gal Gadot is top billed in Prime Video’s real-time action thriller “The Runner.” Per the streamer: “Maia Marten (Gal Gadot) has built her life on being one step ahead — a sharp, resourceful, high-powered lawyer at the top of London’s legal world.  During her routine morning run, a single phone call shatters her world: her son has been taken. The instructions to get him back are simple and merciless — keep moving, follow every command, and tell no one. Stop, and he dies. Forced to sprint through the city and obey a series of sinister commands, Maia must confront an impossible question: how far will she go to bring her son home?”
		
			
			
	Fuze (Sept. 4 on HBO Max)
			
										
					Image Credit: ©Roadside Attractions/Courtesy Everett Collection				
					
				
	A ticking bomb in the heart of London sets the stage for “Fuze,” a taut British crime thriller from director David Mackenzie. Written by Ben Hopkins, the feature stars Aaron Taylor-Johnson, Theo James, Gugu Mbatha-Raw and Sam Worthington. As the military and police scramble to evacuate the city when a World War II bomb is unearthed at a bustling construction site, chaos unfolds across London’s streets.
		
			
			
	100 Nights of Hero (Sept. 18 on Hulu)
			
										
					Image Credit: ©IFC Films/Courtesy Everett Collection				
					
				
	Julia Jackman wrote and directed this adaptation of Isabel Greenberg’s bestselling graphic novel, “The One Hundred Nights of Hero.” Emma Corrin, Nicholas Galitzine, Maika Monroe, Amir El-Masry, Charli XCX, Richard E. Grant and Felicity Jones star. The movie follows a woman named Cherry (Monroe), whose neglectful husband departs after placing a secret wager to test her fidelity. Along with her sharp-witted maid, Hero (Corrin), Cherry must fend off a dangerously seductive visitor: Manfred (Galitzine).
		
			
			
	The Plague (Sept. 25 on Hulu)
			
										
					Image Credit: ©IFC Films/Courtesy Everett Collection				
					
				
	“The Plague” is an unconventional horror tale about a young boy named Ben (Everett Blunck), who is new to the social structure of an all-boys water polo camp. Other children, under the direction of their cruel peer Jake (Kayo Martin) and with very little adult supervision, alienate shy young Eli (Kenny Rasmussen) by saying he has the titular disease. Things get uncomfortable from there. Joel Edgerton co-stars.
		
			
			
	The AI Doc: Or How I Became an Apocaloptimist (Sept. 15 on Netflix)
			
										
					Image Credit: ©Focus Features/Courtesy Everett Collection				
					
				
	“The AI Doc: Or How I Became an Apocaloptimist” explores the intersection of AI development and humanity.  The Focus Features release follows a father-to-be as he tries to figure out what is happening with all this AI insanity, aka the most powerful technology humanity has ever created, and what’s at stake if we get it wrong  Per Variety: “Daniel Roher, the director of ‘Navalny,’ has made a heady documentary that explores the future of artificial intelligence with fearlessly open eyes.”
		
			
			
	Best of the Best (Sept. 18 on Netflix)
			
										
					Image Credit: ©Netflix/Courtesy Everett Collection				
					
				
	“Never Have I Ever” star Maitreyi Ramakrishnan returns to Netflix with the high-energy comedy “Best of the Best.” Per the streamer: “Two childhood best friends, Maya and Anjali, join UCLA’s competitive Bollywood-fusion dance team, only to discover that the road to winning the U.S. Championship is far more raucous and cutthroat than they ever imagined.”
		
			
			
	The Widower: ‘Til Death Do Us Part (Sept. 30 on Netflix)
			
								
				
	Documentary filmmaker Chris Smith keeps his Netflix collaboration going strong after ” Jim & Andy: The Great Beyond” (2017), “Fyre” (2019), “Sr.” (2022), and “Wham!” (2023) with the true crime doc “The Widower: ‘Til Death Do Us Part.” Per the streamer: “In this documentary, a journalist and a detective uncover the truth about a killer whose charm masked a trail of failed marriages and suspicious deaths.”
		
	
	


	
		More from Variety

title: Saylor Hayes’ Death: Officials Release Autopsy Results Of 5-Year-Old As Parents Face Charges
description:
Saylor Hayes
                          Autopsy Results Revealed
                          No Sign
body:
Saylor Hayes
                          Autopsy Results Revealed
                          No Signs of Obvious Trauma
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              
                September 4, 2026
                
                            2:31 PM PDT
                                                                      |
                                                                Updated 
                                  September 4, 2026
                                5:49 PM PDT
                                    
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            The autopsy for 5-year-old Saylor Hayes is complete, and officials did not find any signs of visible trauma, TMZ has learned. 
      
    
            The Georgetown County Morgue in South Carolina conducted the first examination. The officials said Saylor had a strap attached to her ankle that appeared “consistent with a strap of a child’s wrist tether.” 
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            The official told TMZ no “obvious signs of trauma were observed during” the initial exam. 
      

            The autopsy was conducted today at the Medical University of South Carolina in Charleston by a forensic pathologist. 
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            The autopsy revealed Pulmonary edema, which is a buildup of fluid in the lungs. The report also noted there was no external or internal trauma. 
      
    
            The cause and manner of death remain unknown, and a final autopsy report will be ready in 8-10 weeks after additional lab testing comes back. 
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            As TMZ first reported, Saylor's parents, John Herb Hayes III and Geordyn Nichole Hayes, were arrested in connection with her death and are currently behind bars. The two are charged with unlawfully placing a kid at risk/willfully abandoning a child. Saylor went missing from a rental home the family was staying at ... and her body was later discovered in the Waccamaw River.

title: Shia LaBeouf's Alleged Stalker Pleads Guilty, Ordered Not To Contact Actor But Avoids Jail Time
description:
Shia LaBeouf
                          Woman Pleads Guilty To Stalking
body:
Shia LaBeouf
                          Woman Pleads Guilty To Stalking
                          Ordered Not To Contact Actor But Avoids Jail Time
                      
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Shia LaBeouf may be able to rest a little easier ... the woman who had a weird confrontation with him in a parking lot just pleaded guilty to stalking and has been ordered not to come near the actor as part of her sentence ... but she did avoid jail ... TMZ has learned.
      
    
            Court docs, obtained by TMZ, show Alyssa Couture, who was arrested on July 13 in Louisiana after following Shia to a bank parking lot, pleaded guilty to stalking at the recent hearing.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            The judge ordered Alyssa to serve one year in jail but suspended the sentence in favor of giving her a year of probation. Alyssa will also have to enroll in and complete a mental health program and stay far away from Shia.
      

            As TMZ first reported, Shia confronted Alyssa in the parking lot, where he was with his girlfriend. Sources told TMZ Alyssa claimed she was at the bank to close the “demon portal.”
      
    
            Alyssa told officers that Shia was a clone and that the real Shia’s DNA and her DNA were mixed to make the clone.
      
    
            Sources told TMZ that Alyssa had multiple conversations with the police, one where she claimed she was Shia’s wife. She said she was in Louisiana trying to find Shia’s clone, which she felt was being sex trafficked.
      
    
            Prosecutors ended up charging Alyssa with misdemeanor stalking.

title: 'Wheel of Fortune's' Jim Thornton: See Pedophilia Chatroom Photos Behind Suspension
description: These are the photos that got "Wheel of Fortune" announcer Jim Thornton suspended by the show and grilled by law enforcement.
body:
These are the photos that got "Wheel of Fortune" announcer Jim Thornton suspended by the show and grilled by law enforcement.
      
    
            Thornton was on an American Airlines flight back in May from Charlotte to L.A. ... when a passenger eyed his laptop and saw him in a disturbing chatroom. The passenger tells TMZ, she saw images and texts that made it appear it was a chatroom for pedophiles.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            One of the messages she saw said, "Couple of cute boys and a hot little girl." Another read, "All-you-can-eat Boyfett." referring to a restaurant where they could find underage kids.
      

            And there's another message references "CP," which the passenger believed stood for child porn.
      
    
            As a result, the passenger notified a flight attendant and shared these photos with the crew. We're told the captain then notified authorities, and law enforcement met the plane when it landed at LAX.
      
    
            We're told authorities questioned Thornton and he was then free to leave.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Jim’s lawyer, Allison Hart, tells TMZ, Thornton had “become active in suicide-prevention advocacy since losing a close family member to suicide two years ago, and he has spent time visiting chat rooms offering support to individuals suffering from suicidal ideation.”
      
    
            The "Wheel of Fortune" announcer’s attorney said he often visited a suicide prevention website named 988lifeline.org and its chat forum, chat.988lifeline.org. 
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Jim claims he was sent a link to a different chatroom, lifeline.chat, from an acquaintance at the suicide prevention group. Lifeline.chat is for people with pedophilic thoughts ... and has no connection to the suicide hotline chat.
      
    
            The announcer claims he left the chatroom once he found out what it was, although from the timestamps it appears Thornton was in the room for at least 57 minutes.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            His lawyer added that website lifeline.chat is “not unlawful, there is no unlawful child pornography or other pedophilic content, and my client never viewed, downloaded or consumed any child pornography whether on that commercial flight in May or at any other time.” 
      
    
            Jim’s lawyer said their client was never arrested or charged with a crime. His lawyer claimed law enforcement spoke to Jim once he landed and determined no crime had occurred. “In short, my client did nothing wrong,” she said.

schema.headline: 'Wheel of Fortune's' Jim Thornton: See Pedophilia Chatroom Photos Behind Suspension

title: Influencer Rachel Tussey's Doctor Countersued by Surgery Center After Her Death
description:
Rachel Tussey
                          Doctor Countersued By Surgery Center
body:
Rachel Tussey
                          Doctor Countersued By Surgery Center
                          Over Influencer's Death
                      
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            Rachel Tussey's doctor has been countersued by the JourneyLite surgery center, which argues there's no way she overdosed because she didn't respond when Narcan was administered.
      
    
            JourneyLite filed the counterclaim this week ... claiming it is still investigating the influencer's death -- and therefore has refrained from public comment on the case.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            In contrast, JourneyLite says Dr. Shahryar Tork has engaged in "reckless and even intentionally misleading" rhetoric about the case in the months since Rachel passed ... specifically citing an April press conference in which he blasted JourneyLite.
      

            JourneyLite notes Dr. Tork held the press conference only after Rachel's family turned down the autopsy and the body was already cremated ... yet he still insisted JourneyLite gave her too many opioids, leading to an overdose.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            The company also states Rachel would've been drowsy after her surgery if she was overdosing on opioids, but says she was alert and responsive ... adding that employees of the company administered Narcan, but she didn't respond to it, which they insist indicates she wasn't ODing.
      
    
            JourneyLite claims Dr. Tork made these allegations to protect his public reputation. The company is suing him for defamation.
      
    
      
        
              
    
    
            As we reported ... Rachel died back in March following a tummy tuck, liposuction, and umbilical hernia repair. Dr. Tork is arguing she died after JourneyLite gave her a lethal combination of fentanyl and Dilaudid.
      
    
            Dr. Tork says he brought his own suit against JourneyLite "to ensure that the truth comes out and that no other patient and no other patient's family suffers the same tragedy."
      
    
            Rachel was just 47 years old.
      
    
            We've reached out to Tork ... so far, no word back.
